title: Common types of storage
starter: List everything stored on the computer you are using that must still be there tomorrow morning.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Why secondary storage?
facts: It is non-volatile, so data is kept when the power is off.
It holds programs and files that aren't currently in use.
It is much larger, and much cheaper per gigabyte, than RAM.
stations.challenge: Why do computers have secondary storage as well as RAM?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: It is non-volatile, so data is kept when the power is off.
Also credit: It holds programs and files that aren't currently in use.

questions.q: Why do computers need secondary storage?
questions.a: To keep programs and data permanently, even when the power is off
Secondary storage is slower than RAM but much larger and cheaper per gigabyte

stations.name: Magnetic storage
facts: Hard disk drives use spinning platters coated in magnetic material.
A read/write head moves across the surface, magnetising tiny areas as 1s and 0s.
Magnetic tape works the same way, but reads in sequence from a long strip.
stations.challenge: Why are moving parts a problem for a laptop's storage?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Hard disk drives use spinning platters coated in magnetic material.
Also credit: A read/write head moves across the surface, magnetising tiny areas as 1s and 0s.

questions.q: How does a hard disk drive store data?
questions.a: By magnetising tiny areas on spinning platters

questions.q: What is magnetic tape mostly used for now?
questions.a: Large, cheap, long-term backups and archives

stations.name: Optical storage
facts: CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs are read by a laser.
Data is stored as pits and lands burned into the surface, which reflect the laser differently.
Discs are cheap, light and portable, but hold relatively little and scratch easily.
stations.challenge: Rank CD, DVD and Blu-ray by capacity.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs are read by a laser.
Also credit: Data is stored as pits and lands burned into the surface, which reflect the laser differently.

questions.q: How is data read from an optical disc?
questions.a: A laser detects pits and lands on the surface

questions.q: Put these optical discs in order of capacity, smallest first.
questions.a: CD (about 700 MB) → DVD (about 4.7 GB) → Blu-ray (about 25 GB)

stations.name: Solid state storage
facts: SSDs, USB sticks and memory cards use flash memory.
Data is stored as electrical charge in cells, with no moving parts.
Very fast, silent, durable and light, but more expensive per gigabyte.
stations.challenge: Why is solid state best for a laptop that gets carried around?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: SSDs, USB sticks and memory cards use flash memory.
Also credit: Data is stored as electrical charge in cells, with no moving parts.

questions.q: How does solid state storage hold data?
questions.a: As electrical charge in flash memory cells, with no moving parts

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of solid state storage?
questions.a: It costs more per gigabyte than magnetic storage

stations.name: Inside the devices
facts: Magnetic: platters, spindle, read/write head, actuator arm.
Optical: laser, lens, spinning disc, pits and lands.
Solid state: controller chip and flash memory chips.
stations.challenge: Label the parts of a hard disk on your worksheet.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Magnetic: platters, spindle, read/write head, actuator arm.
Also credit: Optical: laser, lens, spinning disc, pits and lands.

questions.q: Match each part to the type of storage it belongs to.
questions.a: Spinning platters and a read/write head → Magnetic; A laser reading pits and lands → Optical; Flash memory chips and a controller → Solid state; A long spool read in sequence → Magnetic tape

stations.name: Choosing a type
facts: Magnetic: huge capacity, cheap, but slower and fragile when moved.
Optical: cheap and portable, small capacity, easily scratched.
Solid state: fast and durable, but dearer per gigabyte.
stations.challenge: Which type would you fit in a school's file server, and why?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Magnetic: huge capacity, cheap, but slower and fragile when moved.
Also credit: Optical: cheap and portable, small capacity, easily scratched.

questions.q: A laptop needs fast, durable storage for its operating system. Which type?
A company needs to archive 500 TB cheaply, and rarely needs it back. Which type?

final.name: Final challenge: sort the storage

questions.q: Is each item magnetic, optical or solid state?
questions.a: Hard disk drive = Magnetic; Blu-ray disc = Optical; USB memory stick = Solid state; Backup tape = Magnetic; DVD = Optical; SD card in a camera = Solid state; Spinning platters and a read/write head = Magnetic; A laser reading pits and lands = Optical; Flash memory with no moving parts = Solid state

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: State what is meant by non-volatile storage.
points: It is non-volatile, so data is kept when the power is off.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

exam.q: Describe how a hard disk drive stores data.
points: It is non-volatile, so data is kept when the power is off.
Data is stored as pits and lands burned into the surface, which reflect the laser differently.
Data is stored as electrical charge in cells, with no moving parts.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Describe how data is read from an optical disc.
points: Optical: laser, lens, spinning disc, pits and lands.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
